While prior frameworks such as the "gut-disc axis" and "gut-spine axis" have addressed intervertebral disc degeneration or vertebral bone metabolism in relative isolation, we propose the "gut-lumbar axis" as an integrative framework that systematically unifies the intervertebral discs, vertebrae, paraspinal musculature, and neural structures of the lumbar spine within a single physiological and pathological continuum. This review synthesizes current evidence on the bidirectional communication between intestinal microbiota and lumbar spine health, covering intervertebral disc degeneration, chronic LBP, lumbar spinal stenosis, and vertebral osteoporosis. Multiple pathways linking gut dysbiosis to lumbar pathology are identified, supporting the gut-lumbar axis as a paradigm-shifting framework. However, large-scale longitudinal cohorts and well-designed randomized controlled trials are urgently needed to translate these findings into clinical practice. Microbiome-targeted therapies, including probiotics, dietary interventions, and fecal microbiota transplantation, hold promise as novel adjunctive strategies for managing chronic lumbar spine disorders, and key knowledge gaps for future investigation are highlighted.

title: CAMKK1 couples STIM1-dependent Ca2+ signaling to mitochondrial metabolic adaptation during osteoclastogenesis
abstract: Excessive osteoclast activation contributes to estrogen deficiency-induced bone loss, but how receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL)-induced Ca²⁺ oscillations are coupled to mitochondrial metabolic adaptation remains unclear. Here, we show that calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase kinase 1 (CAMKK1) links osteoclast Ca²⁺ signaling to mitochondrial responses during osteoclastogenesis. CAMKK1 knockdown reduced Ca²⁺ oscillatory activity, mitochondrial Ca²⁺ responses, NFATc1 activation, and osteoclast formation, whereas CAMKK1 overexpression produced the opposite effects. Immunoprecipitation coupled with LC-MS/MS identified stromal interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) as a CAMKK1-associated protein. Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation and truncation analysis showed that the distal cytosolic region of STIM1 retained CAMKK1 association, while STIM1 depletion attenuated CAMKK1-dependent Ca²⁺ oscillations, mitochondrial Ca²⁺ responses, respiration, and osteoclast differentiation. Forced CAMKK1/STIM1 co-overexpression caused mitochondrial Ca²⁺ accumulation, oxidative stress, membrane-potential disruption, respiratory dysfunction, and apoptosis. CAMKK1/STIM1-dependent signaling was also associated with altered glucose-derived carbon incorporation into tricarboxylic acid cycle metabolites. In vivo, osteoclast-lineage Camkk1 deletion attenuated ovariectomy-induced trabecular bone loss. These findings support a functional role for CAMKK1 in STIM1-dependent Ca²⁺-mitochondrial coupling during osteoclastogenesis and estrogen deficiency-induced bone loss.

title: Targeting macrophage-derived oncostatin M preserves cardiomyocyte mitochondrial bioenergetics and contractile function in fulminant myocarditis
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Fulminant myocarditis (FM) is an acute inflammatory cardiomyopathy with high risk of cardiogenic shock. Current management relies largely on circulatory support, while mechanism-based pharmacological targets remain poorly defined. Methods Cardiac CD45 + single-cell RNA sequencing, whole-heart single-nucleus RNA sequencing, ligand–target inference, spatial validation, and human plasma/myocardial analyses were integrated to define disease-associated cellular interactions. CCR2 + macrophage sorting, macrophage depletion, CVB3-stimulated BMDMs, transcription-factor perturbation, ChIP-qPCR, and promoter assays defined the source and regulation of OSM. OSM signaling was examined using recombinant OSM, OSM-neutralizing antibody, macrophage Osm knockdown, cardiomyocyte Osmr silencing, and STAT3/ERK1/2 inhibition, followed by transcriptomic, mitochondrial, contractile, and in vivo analyses. Results FM featured expansion of CCR2 + inflammatory macrophages, cardiomyocyte inflammatory/stress remodeling, and enhanced macrophage-to-cardiomyocyte OSM–OSMR signaling. Circulating OSM was increased in patients with FM and correlated with higher NT-proBNP and cTnI and lower LVEF. OSM was produced predominantly by CCR2 + macrophages and transcriptionally induced by IRF1 after CVB3 stimulation. Recombinant OSM aggravated mortality, systolic dysfunction, myocardial inflammation, and cardiac injury. In cardiomyocytes, OSM activated OSMR-dependent STAT3/ERK1/2 signaling and impaired mitochondrial bioenergetics, contractility, and Ca² + handling. OSM neutralization and macrophage Osm knockdown improved cardiomyocyte respiration and sarcomere shortening after exposure to CVB3-activated macrophage conditioned medium. In vivo, OSM neutralization improved survival, cardiac function, myocardial inflammation, mitochondrial integrity, and ATP content. Conclusion Macrophage OSM links inflammatory myeloid activation to cardiomyocyte mitochondrial and contractile failure in experimental FM. OSM–OSMR signaling is a candidate mechanism-based pharmacological target for acute inflammatory cardiac dysfunction.

title: In vivo fate-guided design of efficient delivery systems for PROTACs: From molecular rationales to clinical progress
abstract: Despite two decades of intensive molecular engineering, the clinical translation of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) remains constrained by a fundamental paradox: high in vitro potency often fails to translate into in vivo efficacy due to poor pharmacokinetics (PK)/pharmacodynamics (PD) profiles and uncontrolled biodistribution. This review departs from conventional narratives centered on potency by introducing a framework focused on drug fate that explicitly connects the absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion (ADME), and tumor targeting of PROTACs with the rational design of advanced delivery systems. We first dissect the primary physiological barriers that undermine PROTAC performance in vivo, including rapid clearance, suboptimal tissue penetration, and off-target accumulation. Furthermore, we argue that efficient delivery must be engineered from the ground up based on how PROTACs behave inside the body. To this end, we systematically evaluate three tiers of delivery platforms, comprising small molecule prodrugs, macromolecular carriers, and systems based on nanoparticles, with particular emphasis on how each platform can be optimized to overcome specific PK/PD bottlenecks. Crucially, we propose a performance-by-design roadmap that integrates molecular-level innovations with nanoscale delivery engineering, shifting the field's focus from in vitro degradation potency toward predictable in vivo outcomes. By providing rational design principles grounded in the real-world fate of PROTACs, this review offers a timely paradigm shift that aims to accelerate clinical candidate development and unlock the full therapeutic potential of targeted protein degradation (TPD) in cancer.

title: Laminarin suppresses PD-L1 translation by targeting YTHDF1 to exert antitumor immunity in triple-negative breast cancer
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is characterized by low response rates and rapid acquired resistance to current immunotherapies, highlighting an urgent unmet clinical need for novel therapeutic strategies. Herein, we demonstrated that laminarin, a biocompatible β-1,3-glucan extracted from brown algae, exerts significant antitumor immune effects against TNBC with no evident toxicity under the tested conditions. In addition, laminarin suppressed pulmonary metastatic progression in a TNBC metastasis model. Via an innovative in silico target screening framework integrating AI-driven knowledge graph-based causal reasoning with transcriptional signature-based pattern matching, we identified the m 6 A reader YTHDF1 as the key functional target of laminarin in TNBC. Clinical data analysis revealed that YTHDF1 is significantly overexpressed in breast cancer, whose high expression correlates with poor prognosis and tumor immune evasion. We further validated that YTHDF1 directly upregulates programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression in TNBC cells. Mechanistically, laminarin directly binds to the YTH domain of YTHDF1, disrupts its interaction with m 6 A-modified PD-L1 mRNA to suppress both basal and IFN-γ-induced PD-L1 upregulation at the translational level. In vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that the antitumor immune efficacy of laminarin is largely YTHDF1-dependent. Our findings uncover a novel mechanism of action of laminarin, by which it modulates the YTHDF1-m 6 A-PD-L1 axis, providing preclinical evidence supporting further investigation of laminarin as a potential immunomodulatory strategy for TNBC.

title: Leucine-derived isovaleric acid remodels the tumor microenvironment by degrading EIF3I
abstract: Metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion are hallmarks of cancer. Although leucine is well known for regulating protein synthesis, its role in immunometabolic interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) remains unclear. In this study, we found that leucine supplementation significantly inhibited tumor growth. Metabolomic analysis revealed that isovaleric acid (IVA) was the main differential metabolite produced during leucine degradation by the gut microbiota. Mechanistically, IVA directly binds to EIF3I at lysine 17 (K17), increasing its ubiquitination and promoting its proteasomal degradation. The degradation of EIF3I reduces the expression of SMAD3/p-SMAD3, thus suppressing the transcription of the chemokines CCL2 and CXCL12. The decreased expression of CCL2 and CXCL12 reduces the recruitment of myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSC) and restores the infiltration and cytotoxic activity of CD8 + T cells. Overall, our study reveals a novel immunometabolic axis linking isovaleric acid to tumor microenvironment remodeling and suggests that targeting EIF3I may represent a potential therapeutic strategy.

title: Immunometabolism of tumor-associated macrophages in driving colorectal cancer
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality. Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) regulate CRC progression through functional polarization and metabolic reprogramming. Beyond the classical M1/M2 paradigm, single-cell and spatial studies reveal heterogeneous TAM subsets with distinct metabolic programs, spatial organization, and stage-dependent functions. This review delineates how TAM metabolic reprogramming drives CRC via metabolite-induced PD-L1 expression, oncogenic signaling, and crosstalk with chronic inflammation and gut microbiota. We emphasize spatial metabolic heterogeneity, TAM-tumor metabolic symbiosis, the stage-dependent duality of M2-like macrophages in colitis versus CRC, and pathogen-driven cross-kingdom manipulation. Clinical evidence linking TAM metabolic features to molecular subtypes, metastasis, prognosis, and treatment response is integrated, and methodological challenges in distinguishing true metabolic reprogramming from phenotypic changes are discussed. Therapeutic strategies targeting TAM metabolism, including small molecules, chemotherapeutics, TCM, nanomedicine, probiotics, and combinations, are summarized, offering precise TAM reprogramming to reverse immunosuppression and overcome CRC therapeutic bottlenecks.

title: Blockade of mutant RAS oncogenic signaling: A 2026 update
abstract: ABSTRACT RAS proteins (HRAS, KRAS, NRAS) contribute to many physiological signal transduction pathways involving cell growth, cell division, and survival. RAS proteins possess GTPase activity. These proteins toggle between inactive and active forms; the conversion of inactive RAS-GDP to active RAS-GTP is facilitated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) turning the switch on and the intrinsic RAS-GTPase activity accelerated by the GTPase activating proteins (GAPs) turning the switch off. RAS is the upstream component of the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK and the PI3-kinase-AKT signaling cascades. One-fifth of all cancers bear RAS mutations and about 75% of them involve KRAS. Except for the GTP/GDP binding site, RAS proteins lack deep surface pockets able to bind high-affinity inhibitors, which impeded the development of specific antagonists. KRAS mutations occur frequently in pancreatic, lung, and colorectal cancers, which are among the deadliest cancers worldwide. RAS mutations include those of codon 12 G12D/V/C/R, codon 13 G13D, and codon 61 Q61R/K/L. Studies conducted over the last 15 years led to the discovery of the so-called RAS switch II pocket. Sotorasib and adagrasib, which interact with this pocket and directly block the action of KRAS following the covalent modification of KRAS C12, are FDA-approved for the second-line treatment of KRAS G12C - mutant non-small cell lung cancer. Daraxonrasib, which is an indirect inhibitor of wildtype and mutant H/K/NRAS isoforms, is FDA approved for the second-line treatment of all RAS -mutant pancreatic cancers. Daraxonrasib first forms a complex with cyclophilin A (a chaperone protein), which then interacts with active RAS to block RAS signaling.

title: Camellioside A engages SIRT3 to promote FOXO3-PINK1/parkin dependent mitophagy and attenuate UVB-induced skin photoaging
abstract: Chronic ultraviolet B (UVB) irradiation is a principal driver of skin photoaging, characterized by oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, fibroblast senescence, and extracellular matrix degradation. Although Camellia chekiangoleosa shows potential for anti-photoaging applications, its bioactive constituents and underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. Herein, we identified camellioside A (CA) as the key bioactive constituent responsible for the anti-photoaging efficacy of C. chekiangoleosa. In UVB-stressed human foreskin fibroblasts (HFFs) and NIH-3T3 cells, CA markedly attenuated cellular senescence, restored mitochondrial redox homeostasis, and improved mitochondrial quality control by potentiating PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy. Mechanistically, CA directly engaged and activated the mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3, with Gln228 being critical for CA-SIRT3 engagement and downstream activity. SIRT3 activation promoted FOXO3 deacetylation at Lys271 and subsequent nuclear translocation, whereas mutation of SIRT3 Gln228 impaired these effects. Mutation of FOXO3 Lys271 further supported the functional importance of this site in CA-mediated FOXO3 deacetylation and nuclear localization. Promoter occupancy and dual-luciferase reporter assays demonstrated that activated FOXO3 enhanced PINK1 transcription through an AAACA-containing responsive element at -550 to -546 bp of the PINK1 promoter. In a chronic UVB-induced photoaging mouse model, topical CA significantly ameliorated wrinkle formation, dermal structural damage, and extracellular matrix remodeling, whereas AAV9-mediated Sirt3 knockdown substantially attenuated these protective effects and disrupted FOXO3-PINK1 signaling and mitophagy. Collectively, these findings identify CA as a key anti-photoaging constituent of C. chekiangoleosa and establish a SIRT3-FOXO3-PINK1 signaling axis that couples SIRT3 activation to mitochondrial quality control during UVB-induced skin photoaging.

title: Erratum to “Decoding voltage-gated sodium channels structure: Molecular mechanisms linking architecture, function, and disease” [Pharmacol. Res. 233 (2026) 109648]
Prenatal exposure to maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection leads to altered neuro-immune biomarker profiles at birth.
abstract: Maternal infection during pregnancy can induce immune-mediated biological adaptations that influence fetal neurodevelopment. Although vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is uncommon, the impact of maternal infection on fetal neuroimmune signaling remains poorly characterized. We investigated whether prenatal exposure to maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with alterations in circulating neuroimmune biomarkers detectable at birth. In this case-control study, 28 women with SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy and 61 uninfected controls were enrolled. Maternal and cord blood samples were collected at delivery. Following an initial inflammatory screening, neuro-specific biomarkers (NfL, Tau, P-Tau217, GFAP, S100β, α-Synuclein) and PTX3 were measured. Correlation network analyses, PTX3 promoter methylation assessment, and haplotype stratification analyses were also performed. Systemic inflammatory mediators did not differ significantly between groups. In contrast, neonates exposed to maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection exhibited significantly lower cord blood concentrations of GFAP, NfL, and P-Tau217 and increased α-Synuclein levels compared with controls. Tau showed a decreasing trend, whereas S100β and PTX3 remained unchanged. Network analyses revealed reduced cytokine connectivity but enhanced interactions among neuro-specific biomarkers. Although PTX3 promoter methylation was unchanged, the PTX3 h2/h2 haplotype appeared to modulate biomarker interaction patterns. To our knowledge, this is the first study to characterize a circulating neuro-specific biomarker signature in neonates prenatally exposed to maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection. This supports the utility of neuroimmune biomarker networks as translational tools to investigate the biological consequences of maternal immune activation during pregnancy.

title: Mechanisms overcoming the resistance of human TRPV2 to chemical activation
abstract: Transient receptor potential vanilloid 2 (TRPV2) is a thermosensitive cation channel widely expressed across diverse cell types. There, it contributes to numerous physiological processes and plays a role in the pathophysiology of inflammation, immunity, various cancers and neuronal development. The inherent resistance of human TRPV2 (hTRPV2) to stimuli that readily activate its rodent orthologs currently limits progress in translational and clinical research on this channel. Here, we present engineered variants of hTRPV2 that were designed to enhance channel activation induced by 2-aminoethoxydiphenylborate (2-APB), cannabidiol, and the TRPV2 agonist AV2-1, thereby identifying sites that allow for the most effective channel regulation. Through a series of rational mutations and chimeric constructs, combined with electrophysiology and molecular modeling, we identified two key allosteric sites in hTRPV2 that determine the resistance of the channel to activating stimuli. We discovered that two intracellular membrane-proximal salt bridges prevent effective activation of hTRPV2: (i) one formed between residues of the putative 2-APB-binding site and the bottom of S6 helix (R533-E647), and (ii) another formed between residues from the TRP helix and the proximal N-terminus (D655-R369). We also propose possible mechanisms by which the non-conserved pore turret contributes to channel activation. Our results may facilitate the rational drug design towards potent and selective hTRPV2 ligands and help to elucidate the functions of this channel in organs or cell types of interest.

title: Interplay between endoplasmic reticulum stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in inflammatory bowel disease: From molecular mechanisms to therapeutic opportunities
abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are key pathogenic drivers in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Chronic ER stress impairs epithelial barrier integrity and stimulates inflammatory pathways, causing cell death. Simultaneously, mitochondrial dysfunction results in excessive reactive oxygen species production, bioenergetic failure, and defective mitophagy, further disrupting intestinal homeostasis. Notably, these two organellar stress responses are physically and functionally linked via mitochondria-ER contacts (MERCs), which form signaling platforms-mitochondria-associated ER membranes. These platforms coordinate calcium transfer and redox signaling while integrating autophagy and the unfolded protein response (UPR). This review comprehensively summarizes the current molecular mechanisms by which ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction aid IBD pathogenesis, emphasizing calcium homeostasis imbalance, oxidative stress, disrupted mitochondrial quality control, and autophagy-UPR integration. Furthermore, this article highlights the functional interplay between the ER and mitochondria, as well as the MERCs that structurally connect them. Additionally, it discusses emerging diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic strategies based on these mechanisms, aiming to offer theoretical insights and novel perspectives for IBD research and clinical intervention.

title: Mechanisms of lipid droplet-mitochondria interactions and their roles in diseases
abstract: Lipid droplets (LDs) coordinate cellular lipid utilization, energy homeostasis, redox balance, and autophagy through dynamic inter-organelle communication with mitochondria. This review summarized recent advances in the molecular mechanisms regulating LD-mitochondria interactions and discusses how their dysregulation contributes to disease progression. Accumulating evidence has indicated that the contacts between LD and mitochondria are dynamically regulated through specialized membrane contact sites and protein complexes, such as Perilipin (PLIN) family of proteins, Mitofusin2 (Mfn2), and Rab GTPases. Rather than being a passive structural association, this interaction serves as a regulatory hub that integrates fatty acid (FA) transport, metabolic adaptation, and stress responses. It enables bidirectional regulation of lipid metabolism, allowing cells to flexibly and efficiently switch between lipid storage and FA oxidation in response to metabolic signals. Disruption of this inter-organelle communication impairs intracellular lipid utilization, compromises mitochondrial function, and exacerbates oxidative stress and ferroptosis. Such dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a core mechanism underlying metabolic disorders, cardiovascular diseases and neurodegenerative diseases. In the future, integration of protein regulation, gene editing technologies, and precision therapeutic approaches may enable specific targeting of LD-mitochondria communication, thereby offering new avenues for the treatment of relevant diseases.

title: SLMO2 promotes chemoresistance in glioblastoma by regulating BNIP3-dependent mitophagy via the NF-κB/HIF-1α axis
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive malignancy, with chemoresistance acting as a major hurdle that severely limits clinical efficacy and long-term prognosis. Mitophagy, a core mechanism of mitochondrial quality control, enables tumor cells to adapt to chemotherapy-induced stress and maintain survival. However, its regulatory mechanism in GBM chemoresistance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify SLMO2 as a key factor mediating chemoresistance in GBM. Low-dose TMZ induces protective mitophagy, whereas SLMO2 knockdown abrogates this autophagic defense, thereby sensitizing GBM cells to TMZ-induced apoptosis. Mechanistically, TMZ treatment upregulates SLMO2, which potently activates HIF-1α signaling to transcriptionally drive BNIP3-mediated mitophagy, a process dependent on ROS-NF-κB signaling. Notably, this SLMO2-mediated cascade is also engaged under cisplatin-induced stress, indicating a broader role in chemoresistance. Collectively, our findings reveal that SLMO2 promotes chemoresistance in GBM by regulating BNIP3-mediated mitophagy. Targeting SLMO2 disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis by this process, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for enhancing chemosensitivity in GBM.

title: Lentinan-induced FUBP1 O-GlcNAcylation suppresses macrophage ferroptosis and atherosclerosis via the Tp53/SLC7A11 axis
abstract: Atherosclerosis remains a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality, driven by macrophage dysfunction and necrotic core expansion. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent cell death, is a critical driver of plaque instability; however, pharmacological interventions targeting ferroptosis remain scarce. Lentinan (LNT), a bioactive β-(1,3)-glucan extracted from shiitake mushrooms, exhibits potent antioxidant properties but its potential role in the modulation of macrophage ferroptosis remains unexplored. We investigated the therapeutic potential and molecular mechanisms of action of LNT in atherosclerosis. LNT administration significantly attenuated atherosclerotic progression in mice. Specifically, LNT mitigated macrophage ferroptosis by enhancing glutathione homeostasis and reducing lipid peroxidation. Notably, these protective effects were significantly abrogated in mice deficient in solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11), indicating that the effect of LNT is dependent on this molecule. We found that LNT directly binds to far upstream binding protein 1 (FUBP1) and that T559 is required for FUBP1 O-GlcNAcylation and subsequent nuclear translocation. In the nucleus, FUBP1 binds to tumor protein p53 (Tp53), thereby relieving the transcriptional repression of SLC7A11. The resulting activation of the SLC7A11 signaling axis not only inhibits ferroptosis but also promotes scavenger receptor B type 1 (SR-B1)-mediated cholesterol efflux. These findings highlight LNT as a novel modulator of the FUBP1/Tp53/SLC7A11 axis, offering a promising natural therapeutic strategy to stabilize atherosclerotic plaques.

title: FGF21-NR1D1 signaling restrains the CYP4A/20-HETE/GPR75 axis to counteract integrated renal-vascular injury in hypertension
abstract: Hypertension leads to concomitant injuries in the kidney and vasculature, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying this coordinated pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify activation of the CYP4A/20-HETE/GPR75 axis as being associated with coordinated renal and vascular injury in hypertension. In hypertension, this pathway was concurrently activated in the liver, kidney, and vasculature and was associated with renal fibrosis, endothelial dysfunction, and oxidative stress. Pharmacological inhibition of CYP4A attenuated these pathological changes, supporting a functional contribution of this axis to hypertensive organ injury. Genetic and pharmacological evidence further demonstrated that FGF21 acts as an endogenous negative regulator of CYP4A/20-HETE signaling. Mechanistically, FGF21 restored expression of the nuclear receptor NR1D1, which was suppressed under hypertensive conditions, and this effect was associated with reduced CYP4A expression independently of ERK1/2 signaling. The functional relevance of the FGF21-NR1D1 axis was supported by the observation that NR1D1 antagonism largely abolished the protective effects of FGF21. Thus, these findings elucidate a mechanistic axis linking FGF21-NR1D1 signaling to the CYP4A/20-HETE/GPR75 pathway and suggest that modulation of this pathway may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for hypertensive renal and vascular injury.

title: Exploring the role of histone deacetylases and histone deacetylase inhibitors in obesity and emerging evidence from anorexia nervosa
abstract: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) are key epigenetic regulators that modulate chromatin accessibility and transcriptional programs controlling metabolism, energy balance, and reward-related behaviors. Aberrant HDACs activity contributes to metabolic dysfunction by altering adipogenesis, thermogenic capacity, lipid profile, and hypothalamic circuits governing appetite. In obesity, specific HDAC isoforms promote adipocyte hypertrophy, impair browning of white adipose tissue, disrupt mitochondrial function, and exacerbate inflammation and insulin resistance. HDAC inhibitors (HDACi) counteract these effects by enhancing oxidative metabolism, stimulating thermogenesis, reducing adipocyte size, and improving systemic glucose and lipid homeostasis in preclinical models. Beyond peripheral metabolism, HDACi can also modulate neural pathways implicated in food intake, highlighting their potential influence in eating disorders, an area of research currently largely limited to anorexia nervosa. Research on HDACs, HDACi, and eating disorders is relatively recent; therefore, the characterization of potential molecular alterations and the identification of specific HDAC targets remain areas of ongoing development. Collectively, current evidence suggests that selective targeting of HDACs may offer a promising therapeutic strategy to correct epigenetic dysfunctions underlying both obesity and maladaptive feeding behaviors; however, translating these findings into clinical practice will require overcoming key challenges, including achieving isoform-specific selectivity, minimizing central nervous system-related side effects, and establishing efficacy and safety in human studies.

title: SERINC3 promotes oral squamous cell carcinoma progression and mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming involving c-MET/JNK/PGC-1α axis
abstract: Serine incorporator 3 (SERINC3) is a multi-transmembrane protein involved in membrane lipid biosynthesis but its role in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is undefined. Combining clinical specimens with public transcriptomic datasets, we found that SERINC3 was upregulated in OSCC tissues and that high expression was associated with poorer overall survival. Functionally, SERINC3 depletion impaired OSCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, whereas SERINC3 overexpression enhanced these phenotypes. In vivo, Serinc3 deletion suppressed 4NQO-induced oral tumorigenesis, and SERINC3 knockdown reduced tumor growth in both subcutaneous and patient-derived xenograft models. Mechanistically, SERINC3 sustained c-MET expression, and knockdown of either SERINC3 or MET increased JNK phosphorylation and PGC-1α levels; JNK inhibition with JNK-IN-8 partially reversed the phenotypic effects of SERINC3 depletion, while pharmacological PGC-1α activation with ZLN005 suppressed migration and invasion in vitro and xenograft growth in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing and metabolic assays further linked SERINC3 to mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming. Together, these findings identify SERINC3 as a candidate driver of OSCC progression acting through c-MET/JNK/PGC-1α-associated signaling and mitochondrial metabolic regulation, and suggest it as a potential therapeutic target. The precise causal relationships within this signaling axis warrant further investigation.

title: Low-dose juglone attenuates pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy through Lys207-dependent FoxO1 activation and mitochondrial protection
abstract: Pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy is characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance. Here, we investigated the efficacy, safety window, and redox-regulatory mechanism of juglone, a naturally occurring 5-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone. In mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction (TAC), high-dose juglone induced cardiac, hepatic, and renal toxicity, whereas 1 mg/kg/day was well tolerated and attenuated cardiac hypertrophy. Juglone also suppressed Ang II-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in vitro and preserved mitochondrial ultrastructure and mitochondrial membrane potential, respiration, ATP production, and redox homeostasis. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed that juglone reduced stress-associated cardiomyocyte states and enriched calcium-handling cardiomyocytes. Integrated transcriptomic analyses, Biotin-Juglone pull-down assay, surface plasmon resonance, cellular thermal shift assays, molecular docking, and mutational analyses identified FoxO1 as a functional target of juglone. Juglone engaged the FoxO1 DNA-binding domain in a Lys207-dependent manner, and was associated with FoxO1 deacetylation, nuclear accumulation, and transcriptional activation. Activated FoxO1 induced Sesn3 transcription and restored AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172. Sesn3 silencing markedly attenuated juglone-induced AMPK activation and impaired its protective effects against cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction. FoxO1 silencing, FoxO1-K207Q mutation, blockade of FoxO1 deacetylation, or inhibition of FoxO1 transcriptional activity impaired these benefits. Importantly, myocardium from patients with aortic valve stenosis-associated hypertrophy exhibited increased FoxO1 acetylation, reduced cardiomyocyte nuclear FoxO1 localization, decreased Sesn3 expression and AMPK phosphorylation, and increased 4-HNE. Collectively, low-dose juglone attenuates pathological hypertrophy and preserves mitochondrial homeostasis through the FoxO1-Sesn3-AMPK axis, while highlighting the importance of dose-dependent redox effects in determining its therapeutic efficacy and systemic toxicity.

title: Nifedipine-modulated gut microbiota attenuates hypertensive vascular injury through Bifidobacterium-associated inosine-Adora2b signaling
abstract: Although antihypertensive drugs mitigate hypertensive vascular injury, their vascular benefits are not fully explained by blood pressure reduction alone. Many cardiovascular drugs reshape the gut microbiota, which in turn influences their vascular pharmacology. We therefore investigated whether gut microbiota remodeling contributes to nifedipine-mediated vascular protection in high-salt hypertensive rats and a pilot patient cohort. Combining 16S rRNA sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, fecal microbiota transplantation, microbiota depletion, supplementation, and selective receptor antagonism, we found that nifedipine ameliorated gut dysbiosis. Transplantation of nifedipine-modulated microbiota improved intestinal barrier integrity and reduced vascular inflammation, oxidative stress, collagen deposition, and vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) phenotypic switching, while only marginally lowering blood pressure. Conversely, microbiota depletion markedly attenuated these vascular benefits despite preserving nifedipine-induced blood pressure lowering. These vascular benefits were associated with nifedipine-restored Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis 420 (B420) and increased inosine availability. Supplementation with either recapitulated major vascular protective effects of nifedipine without statistically significant changes in blood pressure. In hypertensive patients, nifedipine treatment was associated with higher intestinal B420 abundance and inosine levels. In vitro, inosine modulated macrophages in an Adora2b- and Rap1-dependent manner, with accompanying changes in cAMP and KLF4, ameliorating VSMC dysfunction via paracrine signaling. In vivo, systemic Adora2b antagonism attenuated the vascular protective effects of both inosine and B420. Together, our findings support a gut microbiota-dependent component of nifedipine-mediated vascular protection that extends beyond blood pressure lowering, involving B420, increased inosine availability, and Adora2b signaling. We also nominate B420 and inosine as candidate adjuncts to calcium channel blocker therapy.

title: Alpha-ketoglutarate ameliorates systemic sclerosis-associated fibrosis by restoring endothelial function
abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a devastating autoimmune disease characterized by multi-organ fibrosis with limited therapeutic options. Using targeted metabolomics, we first observed that levels of alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG), a key TCA-cycle intermediate, were paradoxically elevated in bleomycin-induced fibrotic lungs and in TGF-β-stimulated fibroblasts, prompting us to test whether exogenous supplementation could augment this compensatory response. Using bleomycin-induced skin and lung fibrosis mouse models, we demonstrated that oral α-KG administration significantly attenuated dermal and pulmonary collagen deposition, reduced inflammatory infiltration, and improved survival. Although fibroblasts are conventionally regarded as the central effectors of fibrosis, integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and bulk transcriptomic deconvolution unexpectedly identified endothelial cells as the predominant cellular target of α-KG in fibrotic lungs. Consistently, α-KG restored endothelial cell proportions in vivo, rescued angiogenic function and preserved barrier integrity in association with upregulation of eNOS, and tight junction proteins in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) treated with bleomycin. Mechanistically, α-KG suppressed TGF-β/Smad activation and reversed bleomycin-induced metabolic repression, including restoration of fatty acid oxidation signatures and mitochondrial ultrastructure, accompanied by upregulation of the mitochondrial biogenesis regulator NRF1. Collectively, these findings reveal that α-KG exerts broad anti-fibrotic effects in SSc models by protecting endothelial function and inhibiting canonical pro-fibrotic signaling, highlighting its potential as a translatable metabolic therapeutic strategy for SSc.

title: Dysregulated metal homeostasis in Alzheimer’s disease: From pathological modulators to therapeutic targets
abstract: The "metal ion hypothesis" of Alzheimer's disease (AD) has gained widespread acceptance, but translating this understanding into effective therapies remains elusive. This likely stems from a simplistic understanding of metal homeostasis as merely a matter of "excess and deficiency." This article reviews the context-dependent roles of iron, copper, zinc, aluminum, and manganese in the pathogenesis of AD, with a particular focus on their bidirectional interactions with classic AD pathology (the ferroptosis hypothesis is relatively mature, while emerging hypotheses such as cuproptosis have not been fully elucidated). Metal homeostasis dysregulation can directly promote β-amyloid aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell death. Conversely, these pathological processes can also alter the binding, storage, transport, and subcellular distribution of metal ions. Dysregulated metal ions function as "context-dependent" modulators of pathological processes. Their functional effects depend on metal species, concentration, binding state, subcellular compartment, and disease stage. Metal homeostasis dysregulation associated with AD may essentially reflect a redistribution between physiological and pathological pools. Ideal interventions should selectively neutralize pathological metal pools while preserving or restoring essential metal-dependent neuronal functions. By integrating the latest advances in the field of metal-targeted therapies (chelators, metabolic modulators, biomarkers, metal imaging, and gene editing), we emphasize that future treatments should shift from nonspecific metal clearance toward precise metal regulation and precision medicine.

title: Should mitochondrial membrane potential be reconsidered as a criterion of cell death?
Longitudinal proteomics integrated with multi‑omics reveal molecular drivers of responses to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in rectal cancer
abstract: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is the standard treatment for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC), yet its molecular determinants of response remain unclear. We conducted longitudinal 4D-DIA proteomic profiling of pre- and post-treatment specimens from 156 patients, including 31 patients with matched pre- and post-treatment specimens, and integrated with bulk RNA sequencing, single-cell transcriptomics, and functional validation. At baseline, responders were enriched in innate and adaptive immune pathways, whereas non-responders showed proliferative and metabolic programs. Pre-treatment RAC2, elevated in responders, was positively associated with immune activation, oxaliplatin sensitivity, and survival, and was validated in GSE139255 and GSE35640 (all P < 0.05). Moreover, RAC2 demonstrated strong predictive performance (training AUC = 0.867; testing AUC = 0.857). During treatment, NAC induced fibrosis-related remodeling across all groups (all P < 0.05), while responders uniquely preserved CD8⁺ T cell infiltration (P = 0.031). Responders and RAC2-high tumors exhibited concordant pathway dynamics during NAC. Single-cell analysis further revealed that pre-treatment tumor RAC2, higher in responders, transmitted signals to CD8⁺ T cells while receiving inputs from fibroblasts (P < 0.05). In vitro and in vivo, RAC2 knockdown reduced baseline tumor growth but promoted under oxaliplatin (all P < 0.05). Overall, this study offers proteomic insights into NAC in LARC, supports therapeutic decision-making, and identifies potential targets.

title: Pharmacological TRPM8 blockade reprograms patient-derived intestinal fibroblasts and mitigates experimental fibrosis through modulation of myofibroblast activation
abstract: Intestinal fibrosis is a major long-term complication mostly prevalent in Crohn's disease (CD) and remains without approved antifibrotic therapies. Transient receptor potential melastatin 8 (TRPM8) is a pharmacologically targetable ion channel involved in inflammatory regulation, but its contribution to intestinal fibrotic remodeling is unknown. This study investigated TRPM8 association with human stenotic CD and whether pharmacological TRPM8 modulation limits fibroblast activation and experimental intestinal fibrosis. TRPM8 expression was increased in stenotic ileocolonic tissues from CD patients and in primary patient-derived intestinal fibroblasts. In these cells, the TRPM8 antagonist AMTB reduced proliferation and migration at non-cytotoxic concentration and attenuated the expression of fibroblast activation, matrix and myofibroblast-associated markers. In mice with chronic 2,4,6-trinitrobenzenesulfonic acid (TNBS)-induced intestinal fibrosis, AMTB reduced disease activity,endoscopic severity and attenuated stromal remodeling-associated gene expression. Histological analyses further showed reduced tissue injury and collagen remodeling, supported by Masson's Trichrome staining and quantitative analysis of Picrosirius Red. In contrast, pharmacological TRPM8 activation with WS12 did not significantly modify fibroblast proliferation in vitro and/or the evaluated clinical, endoscopic and molecular readouts in vivo. AMTB also reduced the TNBS-induced T helper 17 response without reducing interleukin-23 production by colonic mononuclear phagocytes. Finally, fibroblasts isolated from AMTB-treated fibrotic mice displayed reduced expansion, lower collagenogenic gene expression, reduced contractile/activated fibroblast markers and decreased actin cytoskeletal remodeling ex vivo. Overall, these findings identify TRPM8 as a druggable regulator of fibroblast-driven intestinal remodeling and support TRPM8 antagonism as a candidate antifibrotic strategy for stricturing CD.

title: AI-guided identification of a covalent SMAD3 regulatory mechanism of celastrol in diabetic kidney disease
abstract: Renal fibrosis is a defining pathological feature of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and a major contributor to progressive renal dysfunction. Although aberrant activation of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β)/SMAD3 signaling is a central driver of renal fibrogenesis, effective targeted therapies remain limited. Here, using an AI-guided target-prioritization strategy based on the deep learning platform Uni-Mol, we selected Celastrol for experimental investigation and subsequently characterized its molecular interaction with SMAD3. Activity-based protein profiling combined with a competitive iodoacetamide-based probe assay identified SMAD3 as a direct covalent target of Celastrol, which was further supported by molecular docking and site-directed mutagenesis. Mechanistically, Celastrol preferentially engages the non-phosphorylated form of SMAD3 and promotes KPNB1-dependent nuclear translocation, resulting in the premature nuclear accumulation of functionally inactive SMAD3 and reduced association of SMAD3 with TGFBR1. In parallel, Celastrol disrupts the interaction between SMAD3 and SMAD4, thereby limiting the formation of transcriptionally active SMAD complexes and attenuating profibrotic signaling. Collectively, our findings identify SMAD3 Cys421 as a functionally relevant covalent site for Celastrol engagement and reveal a previously uncharacterized mechanism by which Celastrol regulates the spatial and functional state of SMAD3. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the antifibrotic activity of Celastrol and may inform the future development and optimization of Celastrol-based therapeutic strategies for renal fibrosis in DKD.

title: A trifluoromethylated chalcone derivative attenuates Alzheimer disease-related Aβ/Tau pathology by modulating the AMPK-dependent autophagy–proteostasis axis
abstract: Impaired autophagic clearance contributes to proteostasis failure and the accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ) and pathological Tau in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet pharmacologically tractable activators of productive autophagy remain limited. Here, we screened an in-house library of 64 natural products, semisynthetic derivatives, and synthetic analogues and identified compound 51 (C51), a synthetic trifluoromethylated 4-hydroxy-3-methoxy chalcone derivative, as an activator of autophagy. C51 enhanced autophagic flux, lysosomal activity, and SQSTM1/p62 turnover in mammalian cells and Caenorhabditis elegans, indicating productive autophagic clearance rather than autophagosome accumulation. C51 reduced APP-, Tau-, and TauP301L-associated proteotoxicity in neuronal cells and ameliorated Aβ- and Tau-related behavioral deficits, protein aggregation, Tau phosphorylation, and oxidative stress in transgenic C. elegans. In 3×Tg-AD mice, C51 improved learning and memory, preserved hippocampal neurons and synaptic proteins, and reduced gliosis, Aβ oligomer accumulation, and phosphorylated Tau burden without overt systemic toxicity. Mechanistically, C51 activated AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and suppressed mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations, together with drug affinity-responsive target stability and cellular thermal shift assays, supported C51-AMPK interaction. AMPK knockdown, Compound C, and aak-2 RNA interference markedly attenuated C51-induced autophagy and protection against Aβ/Tau toxicity, demonstrating a conserved requirement for AMPK signaling. Quantitative proteomics further showed that C51 rebalanced TauP301L-disrupted proteostasis networks. Collectively, C51 represents a potent natural product-inspired autophagy activator with therapeutic potential for AD by restoring AMPK-dependent autophagic clearance and Aβ/Tau proteostasis across complementary AD models.

title: Caffeine attenuates Aβ-induced hippocampal dysfunction alongside changes in adenosine receptor-linked GABA handling and neuronal excitability
abstract: Synaptic and circuit dysfunction in the hippocampus is an early feature of Alzheimer’s disease, involving disturbances at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Adenosine receptors (ARs) regulate hippocampal glutamatergic and GABAergic signaling. Caffeine, a non-selective AR antagonist, has well-established neuroprotective actions. We examined whether caffeine attenuates amyloid-β (Aβ)-induced changes in neuronal viability, GABA handling, intrinsic excitability and synaptic excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance, and whether these functional effects occur alongside changes in AR and GABA transporter 1 (GAT-1) protein abundance. Primary mouse hippocampal cultures were exposed to Aβ 1-42 (1 nM) and/or caffeine (0.1, 1, 25, and 50 µM) for culture-based assays, whereas acute hippocampal slices were exposed to Aβ 1-42 (100 nM) and/or caffeine (25 µM) during whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from CA1 pyramidal neurons. In cultures, Aβ increased neuronal death, confirming previous reports, and caffeine co-treatment attenuated this effect. Total GAT-1, A1R and A2AR protein levels were unchanged, whereas Aβ reduced neuronal A1R immunoreactivity; this reduction was not observed with caffeine co-treatment. Radiometric assays identified treatment-associated differences in 1-h 3 H-GABA accumulation and basal 3 H-GABA outflow, including a non-significant trend toward increased accumulation after Aβ exposure and reduced accumulation in the Aβ+caffeine condition. In slices, Aβ flattened the frequency-current relationship and transiently reduced the E/I ratio, whereas these changes were not observed during caffeine co-application; subsequent caffeine exposure restored firing output after 30 min of Aβ exposure. Further experiments are required to establish if changes in A1R immunoreactivity or radiometric GABA handling contribute to the electrophysiological effects.

title: Gut Dubosiella newyorkensis alleviates noise-related atherosclerosis by reducing N1-methyl-4-pyridone-3-carboxamide
abstract: Environmental noise is ubiquitous in daily life and has emerged as a major risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. Nevertheless, the association between noise exposure and coronary heart disease, as well as the underlying molecular mechanisms, remains poorly understood. Here, analyses of UK Biobank (UKB) data revealed that noise exposure was associated with an increased risk of coronary heart disease. We further demonstrated that noise exposure elevated circulating levels of N1-methyl-4-pyridone-3-carboxamide (4PY) in both humans and rodents. Accumulation of 4PY suppressed endothelial NR4A1 expression, activated NF-κB signaling, facilitated monocyte adhesion and inflammatory cytokine release, and ultimately accelerated atherosclerotic progression. Mechanistically, we found that noise exposure reduced the abundance of Dubosiella newyorkensis (D. newyorkensis) in the gut microbiota of humans. Supplementation with D. newyorkensis upregulated hepatic ACMSD expression, lowered circulating 4PY levels, and alleviated noise-related atherosclerotic progression in mice. Our findings provide mechanistic insights into the therapeutic potential of D. newyorkensis in mitigating noise-related atherosclerosis by reducing circulating 4PY levels. Targeted modulation of the gut microbiota may represent a promising strategy for preventing and managing cardiovascular complications triggered by environmental noise.

title: Decoding voltage-gated sodium channels structure: Molecular mechanisms linking architecture, function, and disease
abstract: Voltage-gated sodium (NaV) channels are critical transmembrane proteins responsible for the initiation and propagation of electrical signals in excitable tissues. They consist of a large α subunit and auxiliary β subunits. Together, the voltage sensing, ion selectivity, and rapid gating transitions regulate neuronal, muscular, and cardiac excitability. Recent cryo-electron microscopy breakthroughs have transformed the understanding of NaV structure-function relationships, revealing the asymmetric organization of voltage-sensing domains (VSD), the architecture of the DEKA selectivity filter, the mechanical coupling between S4-S5 linkers and S6 gating helices, and the allosteric mechanism by which the IFMT motif mediates fast inactivation. Across the nine human NaV isoforms, subtle structural divergences underlie distinct tissue distributions, biophysical properties, and disease susceptibilities, explaining the diverse channelopathies that range from epilepsy and cardiac arrhythmias to skeletal muscle disorders and painful neuropathies. These high-resolution structures also illuminate isoform-specific pharmacological pockets, including membrane-dependent cavities in VSD4 and dynamic fenestrations that govern state-dependent drug access, enabling the rational design of small molecules, peptide toxins, and hybrid therapeutics with improved selectivity. Advances in structural biology, biochemistry, and computation have established an integrated mechanistic model that connects NaV channel architecture to gating, inactivation, isoform-specific function, and human disease. This growing molecular atlas now supports next-generation precision therapies aimed at selectively modulating NaV channel activity in neurological, muscular, cardiac, and pain disorders.

title: Comment on "Efficacy of traditional Chinese medicine in managing gastric atrophy and intestinal metaplasia in patients with chronic atrophic gastritis: A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial"
Redox imbalance and epigenetic reprogramming underlie polysubstance-induced neuronal dysfunction
abstract: Polysubstance use is a major contributor to neurotoxicity, yet the integrated redox-dependent mechanisms underlying polydrug exposure remain poorly understood. Cocaine (Coc), nicotine (Nic), and alcohol (Alc) are commonly co-abused substances associated with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuronal impairment. Here, we investigated the effects of Coc, Nic, Alc, Nic + Alc, and Coc + Nic + Alc exposure on redox homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and epigenetic regulation in mice brain and human microglial cells (HMC3). Individual and polydrug exposures increased reactive oxygen species, altered mitochondrial and antioxidant defense pathways, including GSS, SOD2, PGC-1α, TFAM, and Trx/TXNIP signaling. Polydrug exposure further reduced oxidative phosphorylation complexes, altered NRF1/NRF2-mediated mitochondrial pathways, and decreased Mfn1/2 expression in mice brain tissue, consistent with impaired mitochondrial function and fusion. In HMC3 cells, polysubstance exposure similarly increased oxidative stress, as demonstrated by MitoSOX, DHE, and DCFH-DA assays. These redox and mitochondrial alterations were accompanied by changes in DNMT and TET enzymes, consistent with altered epigenetic regulation. Behaviorally, both individual and polydrug exposures produced significant conditioned place preference. Notably, polydrug exposure was associated with reduced tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactivity in the substantia nigra, along with altered dopamine transporter and dopamine D2 receptor expression, increased caspase-3 activation and ASC expression, and changes in microglial P2RY12 expression, together with enhanced neuroinflammatory responses. Collectively, these findings identify interconnected redox, mitochondrial, and epigenetic alterations associated with polysubstance-induced neuroadaptation and neurotoxicity. Although selected molecular pathways exhibited partial counter-regulation, persistent mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammatory responses, and alterations in dopaminergic markers were observed following polysubstance exposure, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for substance use disorders.

title: Corrigendum to “Sinomenine modulates an MGAT3-associated B-cell IgG N-glycosylation pathway linked to macrophage FcγRIII/CD16-related signaling in rheumatoid arthritis” [Pharmacol. Res., 233 (2026) 108458]
GABARAPL1 drives therapeutic differentiation of cancer cells by targeting epigenetic changes regulated by SFPQ
abstract: Differentiation-based cancer therapy is a potentially low-toxicity approach with demonstrated clinical benefits. However, the therapeutic efficacy of differentiation therapy remains limited in tumor types other than acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). Our previous studies reported that diptoindonesin G (Dip G), a natural compound, can induce differentiation in both acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells and basal-like breast cancer cells. In this study, we report a crucial role of GABAA receptor-associated protein-like 1 (GABARAPL1) in driving cancer cell differentiation. By utilizing myeloid cell differentiation models and primary leukemic cells, we demonstrate that upregulation of GABARAPL1 expression was crucial for Dip G-induced differentiation and that Dip G upregulated GABARAPL1 expression by targeting nucleolin (NCL). Also, GABARAPL1 promoted differentiation independent of its autophagic function. Both pharmacological and genetic upregulation of GABARAPL1 expression effectively overcame the differentiation blockade in various tumor models, including AML cells. Mechanistically, GABARAPL1 interacted with splicing factor proline and glutamine rich (SFPQ) and recruited MDM2 to promote the degradation of SFPQ by the proteasome. Upon SFPQ depletion, the transcription of linker histone H1.2 gene was repressed, which in turn rescued the transcription of the differentiation-related pathway. Our study not only highlights the contribution of GABARAPL1 to differentiation but also provides a potential therapeutic strategy aimed at expanding the scope of application of differentiation-based cancer therapy.

title: Polyol pathway inhibition by epalrestat attenuates pathological bone loss through redox homeostasis and sorbitol-linked calcium signaling
abstract: The contribution of polyol metabolism to pathological bone remodeling remains incompletely understood. Here, we examined its role in osteoclastogenesis and evaluated the skeletal effects of epalrestat, a clinically approved aldose reductase inhibitor. Exploratory single-cell analysis of two human femoral-head specimens suggested greater macrophage-associated polyol-pathway activity in the osteoporosis specimen. In primary bone marrow-derived macrophages, silencing of Akr1b3 and Sord produced opposing effects on osteoclast differentiation. Epalrestat suppressed RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis and attenuated bone loss in diabetic, ovariectomy-induced, and inflammatory mouse models under early-intervention regimens. Mechanistic analyses showed improved NADPH/NADP⁺ and GSH/GSSG balance, reduced oxidative stress, and attenuated cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca²⁺ signals and Ca²⁺ oscillations. Genetic and osmotic-compensation experiments further supported a model in which intracellular sorbitol contributes to the osmotic regulation of Ca²⁺ oscillations. Additional findings included reduced inflammation in osteolysis and arthritis models, altered macrophage polarization, and partial preservation of bone marrow vascular features. Together, these findings connect glucose metabolism with redox and Ca²⁺ regulation during osteoclast differentiation and provide a rationale for further evaluation of epalrestat in skeletal disease.

title: The dual role of BDNF in epilepsy: insights from calpain-mediated TrkB-FL cleavage
abstract: Despite the efficacy of current antiseizure medications in managing seizures, approximately one-third of patients develop refractory epilepsy, highlighting an urgent need to uncover the molecular mechanisms driving epileptogenesis. This process emerges from a complex interplay of molecular alterations, involving changes in neuronal signaling pathways. Among these, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its high-affinity receptor, the full-length tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB-FL), are heavily implicated in epilepsy pathophysiology. While traditionally recognized for promoting synaptic plasticity, BDNF signaling can become maladaptive in pathological states. Consequently, BDNF exhibits a paradoxical dual role in epilepsy, acting as a proepileptogenic factor in the acute phase, while exerting antiepileptic effects during the chronic phase. Recently, a calpain-dependent proteolytic mechanism mediating TrkB-FL cleavage, previously described in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and cerebral ischemia, has been shown to occur during epileptogenesis. Elevated levels of the intracellular cleavage product of TrkB-FL, TrkB-ICD, have been observed in the hippocampus of patients with refractory epilepsy, establishing its clinical relevance. In vitro, TrkB-ICD overexpression depolarizes neuronal membranes, increases miniature excitatory postsynaptic current frequency, and alters the transcription of genes related to synaptic transmission and plasticity. In vivo, its overexpression induces long-term memory impairment, a common comorbidity in epilepsy. Moreover, in experimental epilepsy models, TrkB-ICD protein levels correlate with seizure frequency during the acute phase (status epilepticus) and remain elevated during the chronic phase (established epilepsy). These findings highlight TrkB-FL cleavage and TrkB-ICD formation as molecular determinants in epileptogenesis, providing a biological rationale for the contrasting effects of BDNF. Inhibiting this cleavage, using tools like cell-penetrating peptides, represents a promising therapeutic avenue. As the field moves forward, elucidating the precise functions, regulation, and translational potential of the TrkB-FL proteolysis and TrkB-ICD formation may yield innovative, disease-modifying strategies for epilepsy, moving beyond the symptomatic suppression offered by conventional antiseizure drugs.

title: MAMDC2 drives microglia-mediated neuroinflammation via CAND1-dependent IκBα ubiquitination and is targetable by Artemvulactone E
abstract: Sustained microglial activation is a common feature of many neurological disorders, yet the upstream molecular amplifiers that sustain this process remain poorly defined. Our earlier work identified MAM domain-containing 2 (MAMDC2) as an immune regulator enriched in microglia with an established role in antiviral immunity. However, whether and how MAMDC2 shapes microglial inflammatory activation and neuroinflammation has remained largely unexplored. Here, we show that MAMDC2 is strongly induced in microglia after challenge with LPS or HSV-1, both in vitro and in vivo, where it amplifies the microglial inflammatory response. Mechanistically, MAMDC2 associates with Cullin-associated and neddylation-dissociated protein 1 (CAND1) and facilitates K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of IκBα, thereby enhancing NF-κB-dependent inflammatory signaling and activating the downstream JAK2-STAT1 pathway. In male mice, loss of MAMDC2 alleviated neuroinflammatory pathology and glial activation, and improved motor behavior. By combining virtual screening with experimental validation, we further identified Artemvulactone E (AE), a sesquiterpenoid from Artemisia vulgaris L., as a small molecule that targets MAMDC2. AE disrupts the MAMDC2-CAND1 interaction, thereby dampening NF-κB-dependent microglial inflammation and protecting against LPS-induced pathology in vivo. Together, these findings establish MAMDC2 as a previously unrecognized upstream amplifier of microglial inflammation acting through the CAND1-IκBα-NF-κB axis and identify AE as a promising pharmacological modulator of MAMDC2 for the treatment of neuroinflammatory disorders.

title: Mitochondrial transplantation as a therapeutic strategy: From energy replacement to metabolic and immune reprogramming
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction drives diseases, including ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegenerative disorders, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and inflammation. Conventional mitochondria-targeted strategies offer only partial rescue and are insufficient for severe, irreversible damage. Mitochondrial transplantation (MT)-the delivery of exogenously isolated functional mitochondria to injured cells-has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy that directly restores mitochondrial bioenergetic function and may subsequently modify the tissue microenvironment. This Review examines the entire MT pipeline, from mitochondrial source selection, isolation and preservation, to in vivo delivery strategies. We critically examine the multiple mechanisms underlying MT's therapeutic efficacy, including cellular uptake and intracellular integration, energy restoration and metabolic reprogramming, redox rebalancing, remodeling of mitochondrial quality control (fusion/fission, mitophagy, biogenesis), and immunomodulation. We summarize preclinical and clinical applications across multiple organ systems-heart, nervous system, liver, kidney, lung, skeletal muscle, retina-as well as in oncology and aging. We analyze five major translational bottlenecks: the lack of standardized manufacturing protocols, undefined dose-response relationships, immunogenicity and long-term safety uncertainties, the decisive impact of mitochondrial heterogeneity, and regulatory ambiguity. We outline future directions-mechanistic deepening, engineered target delivery, individualized mitochondrial medicine, combinatorial regimens, and a phased clinical roadmap. MT is not merely energy supplementation; it may reshape cellular metabolism, quality control networks, and immune microenvironments, representing a shift from pharmacological modulation of mitochondrial function toward organelle replacement strategies. Despite challenges, these advances may facilitate individualized mitochondrial therapies as a proposed future direction.

title: Shugan Xiaozhi Formula Reduces Hepatic Steatosis and Stiffness in MASLD Patients with Elevated ALT: An Exploratory 24-Week Randomized Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic dysfunction-related fatty liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately one-third of adults worldwide. The most common manifestations in the early stage are liver dysfunction, hepatic steatosis，metabolic abnormalities, and obesity. The failure of single behavioral interventions and the limited availability of treatment drugs remain unmet clinical needs. METHODS: In this 24-week, multicenter, prospective, randomized, open-label, active-controlled, proof-of-concept trial conducted in China, 285 participants with MASLD (ALT >40U/L to 5×ULN) were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive Shugan Xiaozhi Formula (SGXZ) granules or vitamin E 300mg/day. The primary exploratory endpoints were changes in hepatic steatosis measured by MRI-proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) and FibroScan-controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), and changes in liver stiffness by transient elastography (TE) and magnetic resonance elastography (MRE). Additional outcomes included liver enzymes, anthropometric measures, and safety parameters. Analyses were performed in the completer population (n=152) using ANCOVA and logistic regression. RESULTS: At week 24, SGXZ significantly reduced MRI-PDFF (adjusted mean difference vs vitamin E, -3.44 percentage points; 95% CI, -5.18 to -1.69; P<0.001) and CAP (-45.42dB/m; 95% CI, -58.37 to -32.47; P<0.001). A higher proportion of SGXZ recipients achieved a ≥1-category reduction in MRI-PDFF-defined steatosis grade (22.4% vs 5.3%; OR, 5.83; P=0.007) and a ≥30dB/m reduction in CAP (82.9% vs 39.5%; OR, 8.01; P<0.001). Liver stiffness parameters also improved more with SGXZ (TE, -1.14 kPa; P<0.001; MRE, -0.06m/s; P<0.001). Changes in ALT and AST did not differ between groups, whereas GGT normalization was more frequent with SGXZ (52.3% vs 27.7%; OR, 2.87; P=0.010). SGXZ was also associated with significantly greater reductions in body weight (between-group mean difference, -2.69kg; 95% CI, -3.60 to -1.78; P < 0.001), BMI (-0.94kg/m²; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.62; P < 0.001), and WHR (-0.04; 95% CI, -0.08 to -0.01; P = 0.020). SGXZ was generally well tolerated; gastrointestinal events were more common but were mild and self-limiting. No serious adverse events or clinically meaningful laboratory safety signals occurred. CONCLUSIONS: In this exploratory trial, SGXZ was associated with greater reductions in hepatic steatosis, imaging-based liver stiffness, body weight, BMI, and WHR than vitamin E, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings suggest that SGXZ represents a highly promising compound natural medicine therapeutic option for the complex metabolic diseases MASLD/MASH. It meets the urgent clinical need for safe and effective therapies to comprehensively improve patients' conditions. Of course, these findings require further validation in large-scale trials with sufficient statistical power. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ChiCTR2200057595.

title: Striatofugal balance and beneficial effects of facilitating nucleus accumbens mGlu4 receptor activity in the Fmr1-/- mouse model of Fragile X Syndrome
abstract: ABSTRACT Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is the leading monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). To date, no approved pharmacological treatment alleviates social impairments in patients with FXS. Since D1 and D2 dopamine receptor-expressing striatal projection neurons (SPNs) were shown to regulate ASD-sensitive behaviors, we explored whether the balance of activity between D1- and D2-SPNs would be biased in the Fmr1 -/- mouse model of FXS. We evaluated striatal function in Fmr1 -/- and Fmr1 +/+ mice under pharmacological challenge and performed RNAscope® in situ hybridization following social interaction to assess the activity of SPNs in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and dorsal striatum (DS). We evidenced a decrease in D1-SPN activity, biasing the D1/D2-SPN balance. We then evaluated the effects of compounds developed to repress D2-SPN activity on behavioral impairments in Fmr1 -/- mice. Systemically facilitating mGlu4 or blocking A2a receptor activity relieved behavioral deficits in this model. Moreover, social interaction in Fmr1 -/- mice was fully rescued by photopharmacological activation of mGlu4 in the ventral pallidum, to which both NAc D1- and D2-SPNs project, and mGlu4 receptors in the NAc likely contributed to restoring social deficits after systemic mGlu4 facilitation. Together, these results are consistent with our working hypotheses of both biased striatal D1/D2-SPN balance in social deficit and contribution of mGlu4 receptors expressed by NAc SPNs in modulating social behavior. In conclusion, pharmacological compounds able to regulate SPN activity demonstrate a promising therapeutic potential to relieve ASD-like deficits in FXS. Pharmacological compounds ADX88178 (CAS 1235318-89-4); haloperidol hydrochloride (CAS 1511-16-6); istradefylline (CAS 155270-99-8); LSP4-2022 (CAS 1413405-33-0); morphine hydrochloride (CAS 6055-06-7); quinpirole hydrochloride (CAS 85798-08-9); SCH-23390 hydrochloride (CAS 125941-87-9); SKF-81297 hydrobromide (CAS 67287-39-2); sulpiride (CAS 15676-16-1); VU0155041 sodium (CAS 1259372-69-4); optogluram (CAS 1627840-48-5)

title: Targeting the catalytic and ZnF-UBP domains of HDAC6 differentially controls NLRP3 inflammasome priming and assembly in paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy
abstract: Paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy (PIPN) is a dose-limiting complication of cancer chemotherapy driven by macrophage-mediated NLRP3 inflammasome activation. While suppressing TLR-NF-κB-dependent priming can limit neuroinflammation by reducing both NLRP3 induction and downstream inflammasome activation, such upstream intervention may also affect broader immune transcriptional programs in vulnerable oncology patients. Here, we identify a structural division of labor within histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) that pharmacologically uncouples the priming and assembly steps of NLRP3 activation. In a murine PIPN model, we demonstrate that paclitaxel directly primes macrophages. Complementary ND7/23-BMDM experiments support a model in which ATP released from paclitaxel-stressed neuronal cells provides a second signal for inflammasome assembly. By integrating domain-selective pharmacology with genetic knockdown-rescue using catalytically inactive and ZnF-UBP-deletion mutants, we reveal that the catalytic domain of HDAC6 governs upstream TLR4-NF-κB-dependent priming. In contrast, the non-catalytic ZnF-UBP domain is required for downstream HDAC6-NLRP3-ASC complexation and ASC speck assembly, ultimately driving caspase-1 activation, GSDMD cleavage, and IL-1β release. In vivo, targeting the ZnF-UBP domain with CP31 effectively alleviated paclitaxel-evoked pain hypersensitivity and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neuroinflammation without altering canonical α-tubulin acetylation. By reframing HDAC6 into domain-separable intervention points, we provide a pathway-restricted therapeutic strategy for PIPN that precisely disarms downstream pathological inflammasome assembly while largely preserving the measured upstream priming responses.

title: Scutellarin as a multi-target neuroprotective agent: Analytical evidence, pharmacokinetic insights and translational strategies across neurodegenerative disorders
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders are a leading cause of disability and mortality globally, but effective disease-modifying therapeutic strategies are still largely unavailable. Scutellarin is a flavonoid glycoside extracted from Erigeron breviscapus (Vant.) Hand-Mazz. It has been widely studied in preclinical models of neurodegenerative disorders. In this study, we performed a systematic review of preclinical animal studies. We combined comprehensive database retrieval with quantitative synthesis of eligible outcomes. The pooled results demonstrated that scutellarin significantly reduced cerebral infarct volume and improved neurological deficit scores in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion models. It also ameliorated learning and memory impairments in experimental Alzheimer's disease (AD) models. Consistent neuroprotective effects were also found in models of depression, anxiety, Parkinson's disease, etc. Mechanistic analysis indicated that scutellarin produces multi-level neuroprotective effects. It acts by reducing oxidative stress, inhibiting neuroinflammation, suppressing apoptosis, stabilizing the neurovascular unit and other neurobiological processes. This review first evaluated the preclinical efficacy of scutellarin through systematic review and meta-analysis. It then integrated cross-disease mechanisms with network pharmacology, reverse virtual screening and molecular docking to identify computationally predicted targets. Although scutellarin shows promising preclinical effects, its clinical translation faces major limitations. These limitations include low oral bioavailability, poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration and insufficient data on brain exposure. Overall, scutellarin is a multi-target neuroprotective candidate. Future studies should focus on target validation, exposure-response modeling, delivery optimization and clinically relevant translational evaluation.

title: Effects of probiotic supplementation on depression, anxiety, and sleep quality in healthy participants: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of probiotic supplementation on depression, anxiety, and sleep quality in healthy adults. PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase were searched from inception to September 18, 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing probiotics with placebo for ≥ 4 weeks were included. Data from 20 studies involving 1508 participants were analyzed using Stata 17.0. Random-effects or fixed-effects models were selected according to heterogeneity. The GRADE approach was used to assess evidence certainty. Probiotics significantly reduced depression scores (SMD = -0.23, 95% CI: -0.36 to -0.10, P < 0.01; I² = 4.67%) and improved sleep quality (SMD = -0.37, 95% CI: -0.52 to -0.22, P < 0.01; I² = 41.67%). However, the overall effect on anxiety was not significant (SMD = -0.11, 95% CI: -0.31-0.09, P = 0.27; I² = 61.41%). Subgroup analyses were exploratory and unadjusted; no definitive conclusion can be drawn regarding intervention duration or strain type. GRADE certainty was moderate for depression and sleep quality, but very low for anxiety. In conclusion, probiotic supplementation may alleviate depressive symptoms and improve sleep quality in healthy adults, whereas its effect on anxiety remains inconclusive. Larger, standardized RCTs are needed to confirm these findings and clarify strain-specific effects.

title: Unfolded protein response pathway in neurodegenerative diseases: Genetic insights into the mechanisms linking UPR dysregulation to Tau pathology and therapeutic implications
abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress activates a dynamic signaling network known as the unfolded protein response (UPR), which aims to reestablish cellular protein homeostasis and promote cell survival during stress. Dysregulated UPR signaling has been increasingly implicated in neurodegenerative diseases, many of which are characterized by tau hyperphosphorylation, misfolding, aggregation, and impaired clearance, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Genetic variations in UPR pathway components and their downstream effectors may influence the magnitude, duration, and cellular consequences of ER stress responses, thereby shaping disease susceptibility, progression, and therapeutic response. This review examines genetic variation within the UPR pathway and its relevance to the pathophysiology of tau-associated neurodegenerative diseases. By integrating evidence from genetic, cellular, and disease-model studies, we highlight how UPR dysregulation represents an important mechanistic interface linking genetic susceptibility with cellular stress responses, proteostasis disruption, and tau pathology. The article further explores UPR-focused therapeutic approaches, emphasizing how understanding genetic variation may provide insights into disease mechanisms and identify potential therapeutic targets. Building on these findings, we propose a framework in which UPR dysregulation is viewed not merely as a passive cellular response to neurodegeneration, but as a potential mechanistic determinant linking genetic risk to altered stress adaptation, proteostatic imbalance, and tau pathology. Within this framework, genetic variation in UPR components may contribute to distinct disease-relevant UPR states and influence therapeutic responsiveness. Integrating genetic variation with functional UPR signatures and treatment response may ultimately reveal disease-relevant therapeutic opportunities and inform the development of more precise UPR-targeted strategies for tau-associated neurodegenerative diseases.

title: YAP/AP-1 Activation in Sebocytes Promotes CCL5-Dependent Perifollicular Macrophage Recruitment in Rosacea
abstract: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder in which macrophages have been increasingly implicated, yet the spatial basis and local cues of their recruitment remain poorly defined. Given the prominent perifollicular inflammatory changes in rosacea, we investigated whether sebocytes contribute to macrophage recruitment and the underlying mechanisms. Multiplex immunofluorescence combined with distance-stratified quantification demonstrated a preferential perifollicular distribution of macrophages around pilosebaceous units (PSUs) in human rosacea lesions. Integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic analyses identified the C-C motif chemokine ligand 5 (CCL5)-C-C motif chemokine receptor 5 (CCR5) axis as a candidate mediator of sebocyte-macrophage crosstalk. Silencing CCL5 by small interfering RNA and CCL5 neutralization attenuated sebocyte-driven macrophage migration in vitro and reduced macrophage accumulation in vivo. Transcriptomic analysis of sebocytes further linked CCL5 expression to activation of Yes-associated protein (YAP)/activator protein-1 (AP-1) signaling. Consistently, pharmacological inhibition of YAP or AP-1 reduced CCL5 expression in sebocytes and alleviated erythema and macrophage infiltration in vivo. Furthermore, untargeted lipidomics uncovered profound metabolic reprogramming in sebocytes, characterized notably by the accumulation of cholesteryl esters. Bidirectional interventions via simvastatin and cholesterol loading confirmed that this lipid remodeling acts as an upstream driver of YAP nuclear translocation. Overall, our study identifies a PSU-centered inflammatory niche in rosacea and implicates lipid-driven, YAP/AP-1-associated sebocytic CCL5 upregulation in perifollicular macrophage recruitment, providing a rationale for further exploring sebocyte- and pilosebaceous unit-directed therapeutic strategies in rosacea.
