title: Repurposing the orphan drug nitisinone synergizes with sorafenib to sensitize immunotherapy-refractory MSS-CRC via metabolic stress-driven STING activation
abstract: Microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS-CRC) remains broadly refractory to immune checkpoint blockade, underscoring the need for strategies that convert immunologically "cold" tumors into therapy-responsive states. Here, we identify 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD), the rate-limiting enzyme in tyrosine catabolism, as a modulator of sorafenib sensitivity in MSS-CRC. Pharmacological inhibition of HPD by the FDA-approved orphan drug nitisinone synergized with sorafenib across patient-derived organoids, human PBMC-tumor co-cultures, and immunocompetent orthotopic models. Mechanistically, nitisinone imposes strict glutaminolysis dependency, whereas sorafenib disrupts cRaf-MEK-ERK signaling to trigger proteasomal cMYC degradation and transcriptional repression of GLS1, thereby ablating compensatory glutamine anaplerosis. This dual metabolic blockade creates a synthetic lethal trap, provoking irreversible mitochondrial collapse and mtDNA release, which activates the cGAS–STING pathway and drives intratumoral infiltration of cytotoxic NK and CD8 + T cells. Critically, ρ⁰ cells and STING-deficient models confirm mitochondrial damage as the "trigger" of cell death and STING as the "amplifier" of antitumor immunity. In TCGA MSS-CRC cohorts, a double-low glutamine/tyrosine metabolic signature was associated with prolonged survival, enhanced cGAS-STING signaling, and immune-hot tumor features, findings corroborated by single-cell RNA-seq analyses. Finally, the triple combination of nitisinone, sorafenib, and anti-PD-1 therapy achieved superior antitumor efficacy with favorable tolerability in vivo . Collectively, our findings delineate a metabolic-mitochondrial-STING axis and support repurposing nitisinone as a promising translational strategy to sensitize MSS-CRC to immunotherapy.

title: Repeated cocaine exposure and prolonged withdrawal drive morphological and molecular remodeling of hippocampal microglia in response to acute stress
abstract: Repeated cocaine exposure during adolescence disrupts physiological brain maturation, inducing persistent neuroplastic adaptations that evolve throughout withdrawal. Because stressful experiences are among the most powerful triggers of relapse during abstinence, uncovering how cocaine withdrawal affects the neurobiological mechanisms of stress adaptation and emotional responses remains a critical challenge in addiction research. Here, we investigated whether prolonged withdrawal from adolescent cocaine exposure alters hippocampal neuroimmune responses to a subsequent stressful challenge. Male adolescent rats received cocaine (5mg/kg, s.c.) for 15 consecutive days followed by a 14-day withdrawal period. At the end of withdrawal, animals were exposed to acute restraint stress (ARS) and assessed for anxiety-like behavior. Our findings demonstrate that prolonged withdrawal from adolescent cocaine exposure impairs emotional adaptation to acute stress, accompanied by persistent neuroimmune dysregulation across both central and peripheral compartments. Within the hippocampus, a key limbic hub integrating contextual drug-associated memories, emotional processes and stress adaptation, cocaine withdrawal altered microglial homeostasis while reshaping stress-responsive neuro-glial communication pathways in a region-specific manner, particularly the CX3CL1-CX3CR1 axis within the ventral subregion. Stress exposure revealed distinct microglial and synaptic, structural and molecular, adaptations in cocaine-withdrawn rats, characterized by the recruitment of a surveillance-like microglial phenotype and an altered pattern of neuron-microglia communication. These central alterations were accompanied by peripheral lymphopenia and a blunted lymphocyte response to the challenge. Together, these findings support the existence of a latent neuroimmune vulnerability induced by cocaine withdrawal that becomes apparent under challenging conditions potentially driving maladaptive stress processing.

title: Nanomedicine for Alzheimer’s disease: A stage-matched framework integrating pathological network modulation, blood–brain barrier delivery, and clinical translation
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains one of the most difficult neurodegenerative disorders to treat. Therapeutic failure is driven mainly by two barriers: the multifactorial pathological network of AD and the limited access of most therapeutics to the brain imposed by the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Conventional symptomatic drugs and emerging antibody-based therapies provide clinical benefit, but they do not fully address the interacting processes involving amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation, Tau pathology, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and synaptic impairment. In this review, we discuss nanomedicine as an integrated platform for AD intervention. We summarize the major pathological nodes that provide targets for nanomedicine-based therapy and discuss BBB structure and transport mechanisms. We then compare polymeric, inorganic, carbon-based, lipid-based, protein-based, nucleic acid-based, and biomimetic platforms in terms of delivery function, intrinsic bioactivity, pathological modulation, and translational risk. Assisted brain-delivery strategies are also discussed, including focused ultrasound-mediated BBB modulation and intranasal nose-to-brain delivery. We then review clinical-stage AD nanomedicine candidates and summarize the key barriers to their translation. This review integrates stage-dependent pathology, BBB transport, and nanoplatform properties. It proposes a stage-matched framework for preclinical, mild symptomatic, and moderate-severe AD. At each stage, the framework matches active pathological nodes with feasible BBB transport strategies, carrier features, and administration routes. It may guide the development of mechanistically defined, reproducible, and clinically testable nanomedicines.

title: SIRT1 signaling in Alzheimer’s disease: Regulation of mitochondrial biogenesis and therapeutic implications
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is one of the leading causes of dementia worldwide. Its pathological features include Aβ deposition, Tau hyperphosphorylation, and impaired neuronal energy metabolism, accompanied by persistent oxidative stress. As a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + )-dependent deacetylase, sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) is a central regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. This review systematically examines the emerging roles of SIRT1 in regulating these pathological processes in AD, with a particular focus on its regulation of mitochondrial biogenesis. It also delineates the complex regulatory mechanisms governing SIRT1, including NAD + -metabolism-dependent regulation, protein interaction-dependent regulation, post-translational modifications such as ISGylation and nitrosylation, and non-coding RNA-mediated post-transcriptional regulation. In addition, the coordinated influence of upstream activators and downstream effectors is discussed. Impairment of SIRT1-mediated mitochondrial biogenesis may exacerbate neuronal energy deficits and oxidative stress in AD, thereby increasing susceptibility to neurodegeneration. This review further elucidates the molecular mechanisms underlying the SIRT1–mitochondrial biogenesis axis. By integrating upstream activating signals with downstream effectors, SIRT1 creates a permissive regulatory environment for peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α)-driven, mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM)-mediated mitochondrial biogenesis, thereby facilitating quality-controlled renewal of the mitochondrial network. In addition, this review discusses the potential value of dynamic biomarker monitoring following therapeutic targeting of the SIRT1 pathway and summarizes current challenges and future intervention strategies. Targeting SIRT1-mediated mitochondrial biogenesis may provide a promising avenue for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for AD.

title: Gut-Brain coherence: a new therapeutic strategy for stress-related tumor
abstract: Chronic psychological stress significantly exacerbates tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis through neuroendocrine dysregulation and tumor-associated immunosuppression. Beyond direct neural pathways, stress is increasingly recognized as a driver of gut microbiota dysbiosis, which triggers systemic or local metabolic reprogramming, and fosters a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment. Understanding the complex interplay between chronic stress and oncogenic process offers critical insights into the underlying mechanisms of cancer biology. The microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA), as the primary pathway connecting stress to tumorigenesis, represents a pivotal perspective for deciphering this link. Here, we introduce "gut-brain coherence", defined as a dynamic, synchronized homeostasis among the gut microbial ecosystem, neuroendocrine tone, and immune effector function. Based on this concept, we present a dual-direction framework including microbial interventions, behavioral modulation, and targeted pharmacological strategies to re-establish integrated functional equilibrium, offering a unified roadmap to improve survival and quality of life in stress-driven malignancies.

title: Targeting ACKR1+ Endothelial Cells Attenuates Pulmonary Fibrosis by Halting Monocytes Infiltration/Polarization and Endothelial-to-Mesenchymal Transition
abstract: While microvascular abnormalities drive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), the pathogenic endothelial subpopulations and their specific molecular networks are poorly understood. By integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, we identified a pathologically expanded ACKR1+ endothelial cell (EC) subpopulation that correlates with pulmonary function decline and forms a pro-fibrotic endothelial-fibroblast niche in IPF. Within this niche, fibroblast-derived TGF-β upregulates endothelial ACKR1 transcription via the SMAD2 axis. We demonstrate that ACKR1+ ECs promote fibrosis through two distinct mechanisms. At the cellular level, interactome mapping shows ACKR1 drives endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) by competitively sequestering the endocytic adaptor NUMB, which prevents NOTCH1 lysosomal degradation and sustains Notch hyperactivation. In the microenvironment, ACKR1+ ECs mediate monocyte recruitment via CCL2 transcytosis and secrete IGFBP7, polarizing pro-fibrotic M2 macrophages through the CD93/PI3K/AKT signaling axis. Endothelial-specific deletion of Ackr1 protects against bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis. Through structure-based virtual screening, we identified 1F-Fructofuranosylnystose as a direct ACKR1 inhibitor. Pharmacological blockade with 1F-Fructofuranosylnystose halted EndMT and pathogenic macrophage recruitment, preserving lung architecture and respiratory mechanics in murine models, ferret models, and human precision-cut lung slices. These findings establish the mechanistic basis of ACKR1+ ECs in fibrosis and highlight ACKR1 inhibition as a targeted therapeutic approach for IPF.

title: Ubiquitination of retinoic acid receptor alpha promotes severe acute pancreatitis-associated acute lung injury by releasing hexokinase 3 transcriptional repression
abstract: Lung macrophages constitute the first line of defense against environmental attack and participate in the pathogenesis of acute lung injury (ALI). In this study, we sought to elucidate the impact of HK3 on the regulation of macrophage phenotype in severe acute pancreatitis (SAP)-associated acute lung injury (PALI). HK3 expression was enhanced in lung macrophages of mice with SAP, and overexpression of HK3 in macrophages using adeno-associated viral vectors exacerbated PALI progression and increased macrophage M1 polarization in lung tissues. Overexpression of HK3 enhanced the glycolytic activity of macrophages, thereby polarizing macrophages toward the M1 phenotype. Retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARA) repressed HK3 transcription by binding to the promoter of HK3. Knockdown of HK3 inhibited the macrophage glycolysis induced by RARA knockdown and alleviated PALI development. NEDD4L mediated ubiquitination and degradation of RARA, and NEDD4L overexpression promoted macrophage glycolysis-induced increase in M1 polarization and inhibited M2 polarization. In peripheral blood CD14 + monocytes, NEDD4L and HK3 mRNA expression correlated positively with APACHE II scores and negatively with PaO₂/FiO₂, whereas RARA mRNA expression showed the opposite associations. In conclusion, NEDD4L-mediated degradation of RARA hinders its transcriptional repression of HK3 to activate macrophage glycolysis and M1 polarization in PALI development.

title: The hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus as an integrative hub of circadian regulation and a therapeutic target in disease
abstract: Circadian rhythms are endogenous, approximately 24-hour oscillations that align physiology and behavior with the environmental light-dark cycle and support homeostasis. In mammals, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) serves as the central circadian pacemaker, but its neuronal projections are restricted to a relatively small set of hypothalamic targets. The hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) is an important downstream integrative node that receives direct and indirect temporal signals from the SCN and integrates them with metabolic, visceral, stress-related, and limbic inputs. Through functionally distinct neuroendocrine, autonomic, and central-projecting neuronal populations, the PVN contributes to the temporal regulation of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity, glucose metabolism, feeding behavior, nociceptive sensitivity, and cardiovascular function. Cell-type-specific genetic and transcriptomic studies further indicate that PVN neuronal populations exhibit distinct clock-related molecular programs. Studies predominantly in nocturnal rodent models have linked disruption of PVN clocks or rhythmic output to aging-associated decline, metabolic dysfunction, altered tumor immunity, neurodegenerative disease, and pain-related phenotypes. Human post-mortem studies have reported heterogeneous PVN changes in Alzheimer's disease, but direct evidence of PVN clock or SCN-PVN circuit dysfunction in humans remains limited. This review integrates circuit-, cellular-, and molecular-level evidence for the PVN's role in circadian regulation, evaluates interventions spanning timed drug delivery, meal timing, light exposure, and PVN-focused experimental manipulation, and outlines the challenges of translating preclinical findings into clinical practice.

title: UBAP2L O-GlcNAcylation contributes to DDX21-associated stress granule formation and suppression of trophoblast pyroptosis in preeclampsia
abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is a severe pregnancy disorder characterized by hypertension and multi-organ dysfunction. Impaired trophoblast function and defective spiral artery remodeling are considered the central pathological features of PE, leading to placental ischemia/hypoxia and a subsequent inflammatory cascade. Increasing evidence has demonstrated that pyroptosis contributes to placental dysfunction and the establishment of a pro - inflammatory microenvironment in PE; however, the mechanisms remain largely unclear. O- linked β-N-acetylglucosamine ( O- GlcNAc) modification is a reversible post-translational modification (PTM) that plays critical roles in maintaining cellular homeostasis and regulating multiple forms of programmed cell death (PCD), yet its role in pyroptosis during PE has not been elucidated. In the present study, we found that O- GlcNAcylation was markedly reduced in placental tissues from patients with PE and negatively correlated with pyroptosis. In both an LPS-induced PE-like mouse model and trophoblast cells, enhancement of O- GlcNAcylation significantly suppressed pyroptosis and ameliorated PE-like phenotypes. IP-MS identified UBAP2L as a critical O- GlcNAcylated protein. Mechanistically, T446, an O- GlcNAcylation site of UBAP2L, contributed to maintaining its protein stability by preventing ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation and promoted its interaction with DDX21, thereby promoting stress granule assembly. This process suppressed inflammasome activation and pyroptosis, improved trophoblast function, and ameliorated PE-like phenotypes. Collectively, our findings define an O -GlcNAcylation-UBAP2L-DDX21-stress granule-pyroptosis axis in PE and nominate O -GlcNAc signaling as a therapeutic target.

title: Editorial Board
Receptor-Guided Nanomedicine for Rheumatoid Arthritis: Linking Target Biology, Nanocarrier Design, and Translation
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovitis and progressive joint destruction. Although current therapies improve disease control, inadequate lesion selectivity, heterogeneous responses, and systemic toxicity remain important limitations. Receptor-guided nanomedicine offers a strategy to align drug delivery with disease-relevant cell populations and pathological processes. This Review examines how receptor biology and pharmacological characteristics shape ligand selection, carrier architecture, payload choice, administration route, and microenvironment-responsive design in RA nanotherapy. Particular emphasis is placed on folate receptor-β (FRβ) and CD44, which represent the most extensively investigated receptor axes for activated macrophages and broader synovial cell populations, respectively. Representative platforms delivering antirheumatic drugs, glucocorticoids, natural products, nucleic acids, and functional nanomaterials are comparatively analyzed, while emerging targets including scavenger receptors, Fc gamma receptor I, pattern-recognition receptors, and integrin αvβ3 are discussed in their pathological contexts. Key translational issues, including receptor heterogeneity, target validation, formulation complexity, long-term safety, manufacturability, and patient stratification, are highlighted. Linking target biology with nanocarrier design may support more rational development of receptor-guided nanomedicines for RA.

title: IUPHAR Review:PI3Kδ in Cancer: From Biological Functions to Therapeutic Opportunities
abstract: Phosphoinositide 3-kinase delta (PI3Kδ), encoded by PIK3CD , is a leukocyte-enriched class IA lipid kinase involved in immune receptor signaling, lymphocyte development, and immune homeostasis. Its role in cancer varies across malignancies and cellular compartments, involving tumor-cell-intrinsic signaling, regulation of tumor-associated immune cells, or both. PI3Kδ-directed inhibitors have demonstrated clinical activity in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and indolent B-cell lymphomas; however, serious immune-mediated toxicities and infections have limited the clinical use of several agents. This review examines the molecular mechanisms and therapeutic relevance of PI3Kδ signaling across malignancies, distinguishing direct p110δ-specific evidence from findings involving multiple PI3K isoforms or broader pathway modulation. Selected PI3Kδ-directed inhibitors are evaluated according to their pharmacological profiles, isoform selectivity, dosing strategies, clinical efficacy, safety, and regulatory outcomes. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including biomarker-guided patient selection, rational drug combinations, targeted delivery, and optimized dosing schedules, are discussed in the context of available evidence and limitations. Future progress will depend on identifying disease-specific PI3Kδ dependencies and optimizing target engagement to maintain antitumor activity while minimizing immune toxicity.

title: Targeting P23 by PM534 suppresses glioblastoma via disruption of SFPQ-mediated phase separation
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is one of the most lethal human malignancies, with a five-year survival rate of approximately 5% and limited effective therapeutic options beyond standard-of-care regimens, underscoring an urgent need for novel therapeutic agents and druggable targets. Here, we report that PM534, a marine sponge-derived synthetic compound, potently suppresses GBM malignancy in orthotopic patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models and in vitro , with IC 50 value of 1.86 nM in patient-derived GBM#P3 cells. Target identification via activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) revealed P23, a co-chaperone of HSP90, as the direct molecular target of PM534. Subsequent LC-MS/MS analysis, molecular dynamics simulation, and site-directed mutagenesis collectively demonstrated that PM534 covalently bond P23 at Cys58 and Cys75. P23 demonstrated significant upregulation in human GBM tissues and orthotopic PDX models, correlating with tumor progression. Mechanistic studies exhibited that P23 interacted with splicing factor proline- and glutamine-rich protein (SFPQ) to regulate liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Covalent engagement of P23 by PM534 disrupted the interaction of SFPQ with the HSP90/P23 complex, thereby triggering proteasomal degradation of SFPQ and consequently abrogating SFPQ-driven LLPS and oncogenic condensate formation. These findings establish PM534 as a promising drug candidate for clinical GBM therapy and highlight P23 as a therapeutic target in GBM.
